If bank A in Hong Kong gets a check drawn on Bank B in Hong Kong, and the check is in RMB - A will go to the BoC with the check and will get the money, and BoC will take the money from B. text: Germline targeting, though promising, raises several intrinsic challenges that require innovative approaches for practical implementation. One significant hurdle is the identification and validation of viable germline-targeting immunogens capable of effectively binding to the precursor B cells of potential bnAbs. This process necessitates intricate structure-based design and an in-depth understanding of the evolutionary route that bnAbs traverse from germline progenitors to their highly mutated forms observed in natural infections (Haynes et al., 2012; Jardine et al., 2016a). To further refine this approach, reverse vaccinology offers a potential pathway. By deconstructing the process-starting from mature bnAbs and working backwards to infer their developmental lineage-a more rational design of immunogens can be achieved (Kwong and Mascola, 2012). This reverse engineering extends beyond merely identifying genetic predispositions; it encompasses a thorough exploration of the antigenic landscape navigated by antibodies during their maturation process, revealing potential points of intervention where vaccine design can strategically intervene. Moreover, the concept of sequential immunization stands alongside germline targeting as a crucial tactic. Sequential immunization involves a series of vaccinations designed to steer the antibody response through carefully curated intermediate stages-akin to stepping stones-along a developmental trajectory that culminates in the generation of potent bnAbs (Escolano et al., 2019).

Conversely, if no prism-[c] edge dislocations are present then there should be no subgrain boundaries. Our results demonstrate that the density of subgrain boundaries is directly proportional to the density of prism-[c] edge dislocations.
